completedSlices.decision: P1 — applying a deposit settles an invoice; refunding it returns the money. Both are ONE Postgres transaction (owner rejected post-then-update). Owner Option B: refunds use the canonical `payment.record` capability, no `payment.refund`, and the reason is mandatory and server-validated.
completedSlices.what: docs/order-deposit-apply-refund-01-migration.sql adds `order_deposit_balance`, `order_deposit_apply` and `order_deposit_refund` (rev2). Each locks the deposit row FOR UPDATE, validates the invoice (same workspace, same customer, same known currency, final document, a posted invoice entry, real remaining balance), then writes a real `payments` row and — for an apply — its `payment_allocations` row, posts the entry through the real `accounting_post_journal_entry`, records the audit row and the SoD action, all inside one call. A failure anywhere rolls everything back. Repeated requests replay by a UNIQUE idempotency key per deposit; a key reused for a different request — or the same key with a different refund reason — is a conflict. `order_deposits` gained `currency`, `posting_status` (`posted` | `pending_posting`, NULL = written before the column) and `journal_entry_id`; a deposit whose receipt never posted is refused and can be recovered through POST …/post. REFUND REASON (owner Option B): mandatory, trimmed 3..500 characters, validated in SQL and in the reusable domain schema; the old 11-argument refund function is DROPPED so it cannot be bypassed; the reason is stored on `order_deposit_refunds.reason` and copied into `audit_logs.new_data` together with actor_id, occurred_at, amount, currency, deposit_id, payment_id and journal_entry_id. A refund row is written only after the posted journal entry is re-read (`DEPOSIT_REFUND_NOT_POSTED` otherwise), inside the same transaction.

decisions.why: The business profile is stored per USER (profiles.business_types, backend/src/routes/auth.routes.ts:203-213), and the UI reads the signed-in user's own row. A backend guard needs ONE authoritative profile per workspace; the choice (owner's profile? a new workspaces column?) changes who may use a feature in a multi-user business and would newly lock out API clients on a generic profile. NEW EVIDENCE: the repository already contains a workspace-level design (migration above) that nothing consumes, AND an invariant that contradicts the V53 mission item "backend must reject operations that need an unavailable capability": IMPLEMENTATION-MAP invariant 1 says business-profile policy NEVER changes authorization or role capabilities ("emphasis only"). evidence: docs/business-profile-01-migration.sql:1-20 (2026-10-27: columns workspaces.business_types / operating_characteristics, "moves business profile from user account to workspace"; no backend or UI code reads them)

decisions.decision: Cycle count completion is idempotent and warehouse-scoped, but not a single database transaction.
decisions.why: supabase-js has no transaction. Idempotency (skip products that already have a movement for the count) plus the cycle-count-02 unique index make a retry or a race safe; a crash between the movements and the status close leaves a counting count that a retry finishes. A true single-transaction RPC needs the priced lines passed in and the costing core unchanged; deferred to avoid an unverified plpgsql function (PostgreSQL is BLOCKED_EXTERNAL).

decisions.decision: Audit hash writer deferred (design recorded, not coded).
decisions.why: The reader (AuditService.verifyChain) hashes a created_at string that JavaScript and PostgreSQL format differently, so a correct writer must live in the database (BEFORE INSERT trigger with a per-workspace advisory lock) and the verifier must be a SQL function the service calls. That replaces the logic the current audit.test.ts exercises, so the old tests must be re-expressed, not weakened; needs its own migration, VERIFY and scenario proof.
